summary: Describes how to safely replace the certificates that BGPsec routers use to sign routing announcements. The rollover must keep the distribution of new public keys in step with signed BGP updates so that verification keeps working. It also explains when and why a rollover is needed, so routing information is not lost.

plainLanguage.summary: Changing the lock on a door only works if everyone gets the new key before the old one stops working. This explains how to swap router keys so nobody gets locked out.

questions: how to roll over router keys
how to roll over bgpsec router certificate
when should a bgpsec router certificate be replaced
subtitle: How to swap the keys a BGPsec router signs with, without breaking route verification.

tldr.problem: BGPsec routers sign their routing updates with a private key, and other routers verify them with a matching public key from a certificate. If the key is replaced before verifiers have the new certificate, valid updates look invalid.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a five-step rollover: publish the new certificate, wait through a staging period, switch to the new key and re-sign updates, optionally revoke the old certificate, then withdraw the old key from routers.
tldr.outcome: Followed carefully, the rollover happens without routing information being lost. It can also be used to invalidate replayed or stale updates.

facts.label: Replay window requirement
facts.value: On the order of a day or longer

facts.label: Minimum replay window
facts.value: 2x propagation time, or 1x if provisioned ahead

today: RFC 8634 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 224, August 2019) and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is the reference procedure for rolling BGPsec router certificates, alongside RFC 8635 on router keying.

sections.title: Why Router Keys Must Be Rolled Over
sections.content:
In BGPsec, a key rollover (or re-key) means changing a router's key pair, issuing the matching new router certificate and, if the old certificate is still valid, revoking it. It has to happen at regular intervals, normally because of the local network's policies.

The danger is timing. Once the old certificate stops being valid, any BGPsec UPDATE message signed with the old key becomes invalid. A router that does not refresh its outbound updates may therefore see previously sent routing information treated as unauthenticated. So the new certificates must be distributed throughout the RPKI before the router starts signing with the new private key.

The RFC only covers changing a router's BGPsec key pair. Rolling over the RPKI Certification Authority key pairs is covered by RFC 6489.
sections.plainLanguage: If you change the lock before your friends have the new key, they cannot get in. So you hand out new keys first, and only then swap the lock.

sections.title: When a Certificate Should Be Replaced
sections.content:
A BGPsec router certificate SHOULD be replaced when certain events occur, and it can be replaced for any other reason at the discretion of the AS responsible for it. The RFC lists four:

  • Scheduled rollover: certificates have an expiration date (NotValidAfter), so they must be refreshed or reissued often.
  • Router certificate field changes: information such as the Autonomous System Number or the Subject may need to change.
  • Emergency rollover: special circumstances such as a compromised key.
  • Protection against withdrawal suppression and replay attacks: if an AS finds that withdrawn updates are being propagated instead of the latest ones, changing the key and revoking the old certificate invalidates the replayed updates.

In some cases a new certificate can be issued without changing the key pair. That is simpler, because receivers do not even need to notice. But keeping a key for a long time raises the risk that a compromised key is used to send false updates. Reusing the old public key in a new certificate is NOT RECOMMENDED after a key compromise, or when withdrawn updates are suspected of being distributed.
sections.plainLanguage: You change a key when it is about to expire, when the label on it is wrong, when it might have been stolen, or when someone keeps using an old copy.

sections.title: The Five-Step Rollover Process
sections.content:
The process depends on how keys are provisioned in the AS. An automatic mechanism such as EST (RFC 7030) allows automatic re-keying at minimum development cost. The safe process is:

  1. New Certificate Publication. Generate a new key pair if needed, create a new certificate and publish it at the right RPKI repository publication point.
  2. Staging Period. Wait while RPKI caches around the globe fetch the new certificate. The minimum depends on the interval between repository fetches. An administrator who rolls over often can provision two certificates per router with different valid start times, so relying parties already hold the next public key. Without that, an emergency rollover may have no staging period, and routing may be disrupted because routers cannot validate updates signed with the new key.
  3. Twilight. The speaker stops signing with the old key and starts with the new one, generating refreshed BGPsec UPDATE messages. This may produce many messages, so a speaker may skew the timing for different peers, for example by a few minutes each.
  4. Certificate Revocation. Optional, but it SHOULD be done when the goal is to invalidate updates signed with the old key, for instance after a suspected compromise. The CA MAY publish the old serial number on its CRL, or simply let the certificate expire.
  5. RPKI-Router Protocol Withdrawals. When the old certificate's validity ends, relying parties tell their routers the old public key is no longer valid (for example with the protocol in RFC 8210). A router's reaction SHOULD include removing RIB entries signed with that key and generating matching BGP UPDATE messages with Withdrawn Routes.

The mechanism depends on automatic provisioning and on a staging time based on RPKI propagation time (at the time of writing, typically a 24-hour period). An AS is REQUIRED to re-sign all originated and transited updates that were signed with the old key.
sections.plainLanguage: First you post the new key where everyone can pick it up. You wait until they have. Then you switch, maybe cancel the old key, and finally everyone throws the old key away.

sections.title: Planning Ahead and Reusing Keys
sections.content:
The first two steps, publication and staging, may happen in advance of the rest. That lets a network operator carry out the actual switch quickly when the time comes.

If a new certificate is generated without changing the key, steps 3 (Twilight) and 5 (RPKI-Router Protocol Withdrawals) SHOULD NOT be executed, since the key that signs and verifies has not changed.

An emergency rollover is the hard case. If the next certificate was not provisioned in advance, there may be no staging period, and routers may be unable to validate updates signed with the new key.
sections.plainLanguage: If you hand out the spare keys early, switching later is quick. If you keep the same key and only change the label, nobody has to do anything.

sections.title: Rollover as a Defence Against Replay Attacks
sections.content:
Two common ways to stop replay attacks are timestamps and serial numbers, but neither BGP nor BGPsec has them. A timestamp approach was originally proposed for BGPsec but was dropped in favour of key rollover. By re-keying, an AS lets the certificate validation time act as a kind of timestamp.

A replay is only effective in specific circumstances: a downstream topology change has made the signed AS path out of date, and that change makes the replayed route preferable to the new one. With no topology change, a replay is harmless because the signed information is still valid. RFC 8207 says the window of exposure requirement is in the order of a day or longer, which makes rollover feasible. The old and new certificates must not share the same key for this to work.

A transit AS that also originates its own prefixes and wants replay protection for them SHOULD have two unique key pairs and certificates. One signs updates for its own prefixes and can have a replay protection policy. The other signs transit updates and SHOULD NOT have one, because rolling keys for everything would generate a large number of updates across the Default-Free Zone.

Advantages: expiration policies stay in the RPKI; much of the extra cost falls on the provider that wants the protection; and re-keying can be coordinated with planned topology changes, such as changing providers.

Disadvantages: frequent rollovers add administrative and BGP processing load; the minimum replay window is bounded by RPKI propagation time (2x, or 1x if provisioned ahead of time, because first the new certificate and then the CRL must propagate); and re-keying increases the dynamics and size of the RPKI repository.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone keeps replaying an old message, changing the secret stamp makes every old message with the old stamp worthless. The catch is that changing stamps all the time is a lot of work.

sections.title: Process Risks and Scope
sections.content:
This document does not change the RPKI or BGPsec. It describes a process for managing BGPsec router certificates within the RPKI. Because rolling over signing keys also invalidates signatures made with the old key, the rollover must be carefully orchestrated so that valid updates are not treated as invalid, which could affect Internet routing.

The RFC 8635 operator-driven method lets a key pair be shared among multiple BGP speakers. In that case, rolling over the certificate affects every speaker that shares the private key. The RFC also states it has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: If several routers share one key, changing it changes it for all of them, so you have to plan for the whole group at once.

viz.caption: THE FIVE ROLLOVER STEPS IN ORDER (RFC 8634)

items.title: 1. New Certificate Publication
items.text: Publish the new certificate at the RPKI repository publication point.

items.title: 2. Staging Period
items.text: Wait for RPKI caches to fetch the new certificate.

items.title: 3. Twilight
items.text: Stop signing with the old key, start with the new one.

items.title: 4. Certificate Revocation
items.text: Optional: revoke the old certificate via the CRL.

items.title: 5. RPKI-Router Protocol Withdrawals
items.text: Routers drop the old key and updates signed with it.
